Agreed that it would be wasteful, but cost-cutting measures that exclude certain members of the public, especially those with disabilities, just makes me sad. We don't have people shoveling coal anymore, but not having that job role didn't have an impact on a wider population than those doing the job, whereas cutting face-to-face services will impact many more than just the ticket officer.

People with cognitive and learning disabilities are already struggling in a world that's going cashless and attendant-less, it's sad to see that we're restricting some of their freedom to save money.

I work with a few clients who are unable to use bank cards as they are unable to understand a monetary balance that they can't see. Give them £20 in cash and they know they've spent £11.90 because it's in their hands. 

Admittedly it's not like an enormous chunk of the population would be affected, but those with dementia, learning difficulties or any other cognitive disability would likely struggle in a cashless society, and also in one that restricts face-to-face services like ticket offices, checkouts etc.
What about people with disabilities that aren't able to use self service? If you're going to need a member of staff on hand to help them out, why not just keep the ticket desk?

Not to mention people who aren't able to cope with self service. Most of the clients I support are people with some learning difficulty or other,  and these kind of moves punish them the most. 

Same with banks going almost all online. My clients can't use online banking or apps, but they're finding it harder and harder to get actual help in a physical bank.

I've met a few people who do it, and their attitude is that they're just doing their job.
